newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr dips, wage deal stirs rate suspicion.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr dips, wage deal stirs rate suspicion.

text.p: The Australian dollar faltered Tuesday as the market mulled over the mixed implications of an inflation-friendly minimum wage award.

The weekly wage rise of just A$10 compared to a union claim of A$20 and analysts expectations of A$12. The latter reckoned this would be a big relief to the Reserve Bank and the money market agreed, taking bond and bill yields sharply lower.

The deal boded well for keeping inflation low and, in the long run, was likely to boost offshore confidence in bonds and the dollar. But it also stoked speculation of another cut in official rates and that had to be bearish for the A$ near term.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the local dollar had faded to US$0.7755/60 from US$0.7785/90 just before the wage news broke, but was not that far from Monday's late US$0.7765/70.

Support was well defined at US$0.7720 after surviving a few days of downside pressure, while resistance was proving stubborn in the US$0.7785/95 band. A break of either was expected to trigger a quick stop-loss move with US$0.7680 and US$0.7820 the immediate targets.
Dealers said the immediate response to the wage deal was muted, perhaps as the market had fretted over it for so long, but felt offshore investors would sell once the news sunk in.
"There were a few factors propping the AUD up," said Andrew McGill, a forex sales dealer at Chase, referring to a 25 billion yen dual currency bond and buying for some expiring options.
"But once those fade, the market will focus on CPI data tomorrow, which it suspects will be low and will encourage the RBA to maybe ease again," he said.

The consumer price figures on Wednesday are widely expected to show inflation pressure remained subdued in the March quarter with the headline growth rate slowing to a four-year low of 1.2 percent from 1.5 percent in Q4. The key core rate is seen steady at 2.1 percent, the bottom of the RBA's 2-3 percent target band.
Today's modest wage deal had removed a potential danger to the inflation outlook, given the RBA reckoned granting the full claim would have added at least 1.6 percent to wage growth.

Andrew Pease, chief economist at Nomura Australia, said the A$10 actually granted would add only 0.4 percent to wages and points to aggregate wages growth of around 4.1 percent, within the RBA's 4.5-5.0 percent comfort zone.

"The decision removes one of the major threats to the medium term inflation outlook and increases the chances of a further interest rate cut," said Pease. The futures market seemed to agree and the June bill jumped eight basis points to 94.11.
That implied a rate of 5.89 percent compared to the present official cash rate fo 6.00 percent, indicating investors were beginning to think an easing was really possible.
Falling money market rates were reflected in forward rates for the dollar which blew out to an 11.5/14.5 premium, the highest levels in over a decade.

Australian one and two year bond yields had fallen below those in the U.S. and the trend was set to continue with the market expecting the Federal Reserve to hike its funds rate to 5.75 percent in May. If the RBA did cut, it would take domestic rates under the U.S. for the first time since the early 1980s.

But Nomura's Pease still doubted the RBA would take the plunge. "For one thing, it would require the RBA to downgrade its optimistic economic outlook," he said. "And it would need signs the Fed was unlikely to hike, or the RBA risked a sharp correction in the AUD if it eased."
He looked for rates to stay unchanged for the rest of 1997 before moving higher in early 1998.
"The main imapct of today's wage decision could be to extend the period of time the RBA can leave rates at six percent,"
On the crosses, the dollar had edged up to 97.67/77 yen from 97.45/55 and to 60.1 in trade weighted terms from 60.0.
The dollar was aided on the yen by news the New South Wales Treasury Corp was launching a 25 billion yen dual currency bond, the first yen/A$ issue in some time.
The supportive impact of the A$4.85 billion Victorian power station sale was fading fast, however, eith dealers guessing the U.S. bidders had covered what A$ exposure they had.

As many suspected, the forex effect of the sale was limited by the fact the greater part of the payment -- around A$3.6 billion -- was funded by debt issued in Australia. A source said the exposure was only around A$500 million and dealers reckoned much of that had been covered Monday. -- Wayne Cole 9373 1800
